title: Base64 Logit Weights and Their Conditional Strip
takeaway: For the base64 feature A/1/2357, the tokens whose logits it raises shade gradually from ordinary text tokens into base64-specific ones, rather than separating into two clean groups. The narrow strip below the histogram makes this visible by showing, at each logit weight, only the mix of token types and not how many tokens there are.
walkthrough:
You are looking at one figure with two panels sharing an x-axis. The tall panel is a histogram over the vocabulary. The thin band underneath is the "conditional" the surrounding text points to.

### What is being counted

Every vocabulary entry gets one number: the [[logit-weight]] of the base64 feature [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 on that token. It says how much that token's output logit moves when the feature fires. The tall panel plots the distribution of those numbers, with horizontal position the weight and height the number of vocabulary entries there.

Color is a property of the *token*, not of the feature. Each token string $s$ is scored by the [[base64-proxy]], a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s))$. Deep blue is $-5$: the string is much likelier in ordinary text than in a base64 dump. Deep red is $+5$: the reverse. Each histogram bar is stacked by that score, reddest at the bottom.

Read the tall panel first. The bulk sits at zero and is solid blue, and the authors tag it "Interference Weights?" — a hedged guess that these tiny weights are cross-talk forced by [[superposition]] rather than anything deliberate [[weight-interference]]. To the right there is a shoulder and a small bump near $0.3$, magnified in the inset.

### What the strip adds

The strip has the same x-axis, but each vertical slice is stretched to fill the height. It throws away the count and keeps only the composition: among tokens with this logit weight, what fraction has which proxy score. Regions holding a handful of tokens get the same visual weight as the peak.

So read it left to right. It is solid blue out to roughly zero, then slides through pale blue, then pink, and only reaches saturated red near $0.35$–$0.4$.

That slide is the point. The same strip for the [[arabic-script-feature]] is blue and then abruptly red — a step. The paper's reading is that a token is Arabic or not, close to binary, while base64-ness is graded: `fr` is a French abbreviation *and* a legal base64 pair, so the model has reason to raise it only a little.

terms.definition: The figure's title. It names the object plotted: the spread of one feature's influence on next-token logits, taken across every vocabulary entry.
The feature being plotted, in the paper's naming scheme: transformer A, dictionary-learning run 1, feature index 2357. This is the base64 feature.

terms.term: "Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element"
terms.definition: The subtitle. It states the unit of the histogram: one data point per vocabulary element, not per token occurrence in the corpus.

For one feature and one vocabulary token, a linear estimate of how much the feature firing pushes that token's logit up or down. It is computed by multiplying the feature's direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding matrix.
The horizontal axis of both panels, in logit units. Positive means the feature makes that token more likely; negative means less likely.

The vertical axis of the tall panel: how many vocabulary entries per unit of logit weight sit at that position. Its integral over the axis is the number of vocabulary entries included, so the tick values are far larger than the vocabulary itself.
One entry in the model's token vocabulary. The histogram has one sample per element, so a token that is common in text counts exactly as much as a token that almost never appears.

An annotation, with the question mark left in, pointing at the large blue mode centered on zero. The authors suspect these near-zero weights are unwanted cross-talk from packing many features into few dimensions, not anything the feature is trying to do.

The material to the right of the central peak — the shoulder near 0.1 and the bump near 0.3. For every feature the paper studies in depth, this far-right group turns out to be tokens specific to the feature's context.

terms.term: "Note the bump in the right tail, which corresponds to base64 tokens."
terms.definition: The note above the inset. It asserts that the small far-right hump is made of base64-specific tokens, which the coloring is meant to support.

The magnified box at upper right, redrawing the region from logit weight 0.2 to 0.6 on a vertical scale of roughly the bottom 45K of the main panel. Without it the second mode is only a few pixels tall.
The color scale. It maps each token's base64 proxy score to a color, running blue through white to red.
The arrow on the legend, saying which end of the color scale is which. Red is the base64 end; blue means the token is more characteristic of ordinary text.

The score coloring every token here: log of P(string | base64) over P(string). The numerator models base64 as characters drawn uniformly from [a-zA-Z0-9+/]; the denominator is the string's probability under the ordinary data distribution.
The denominator of the proxy, estimated as the product of independent unigram token probabilities over the string. A string that is common in the corpus gets a large P(s) and therefore a blue score.
The flat band below the histogram. At each logit weight it stretches the color stack to full height, so it shows the proportions of proxy scores at that weight and discards how many tokens are there.

The leftmost label group in the inset, listing tokens found around logit weight 0.24. The stack there is still part blue: these are short strings that occur freely in ordinary text, and '=-' is not even legal base64.

The middle label group, around logit weight 0.35. These are two-character letter pairs, several mixing cases, that are rare in English but ordinary inside base64 — the stack there is almost entirely red.
The label group at the far right tail, the tokens this feature raises most. They are short base64-legal strings with low unigram probability, so the proxy scores them at the red end.

The comparison case, whose version of this same plot appears earlier in the paper. Its conditional strip switches from blue to red abruptly, which is what makes the base64 gradient worth pointing out.
Cross-talk between features whose directions cannot all be orthogonal, so activating one slightly moves others. It is the paper's proposed source of the large central mode of near-zero weights.
Softmax is shift-invariant, so logit weights have no absolute zero. The paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero, which is why the central mode sits at the origin.

numbers.meaning: The feature identifier, read in three parts: the transformer it came from (A), the dictionary-learning run (1, which fixes the dictionary size and L1 coefficient), and the index of the feature within that run (2357).
The x-axis range in logit units, tick-marked every 0.1. The weights are small because they are one feature's linear contribution to a logit, not the logit itself.

The y-axis ticks of the tall panel, in vocabulary entries per unit logit weight. They are in the hundreds of thousands because the distribution is squeezed into a range about 0.2 wide, so the height times that width recovers a vocabulary of tens of thousands.
The height of the central peak, the tallest point in the figure. Almost the whole vocabulary is barely affected by this feature, which is what the peak's height encodes.
Where the central peak sits, just right of zero. Zero is the median weight by construction, and the mode landing slightly above it reflects the right skew the text describes.
The median logit weight, set by the paper's centering convention rather than measured. Because softmax ignores a constant added to all logits, only differences between these weights carry meaning.
Where the shoulder of paler blue and pink begins in the tall panel. The text calls this side base64-neutral or slightly base64-leaning, not yet base64-specific.
Where the small bump in the right tail sits, the mode the inset's note attributes to base64 tokens.
The x-range redrawn by the inset. It starts where the central mode has essentially died out, so the inset is showing only the second mode.

The approximate top of the inset's vertical scale, read off the dashed guide in the main panel — roughly the bottom fifth of the 0.25M axis. The second mode is small enough that it needs this much magnification to be legible.

The range of the color scale, in nats of log-likelihood ratio, with ticks at -2.5, 0 and 2.5. Zero (white) means the string is equally likely under base64 and under ordinary text; +5 means about 150 times likelier under base64.
The probability the proxy assigns to each character inside a base64 string, since base64 uses 64 characters. A two-character token that is entirely base64-legal therefore gets a numerator of 1/4096.
The probability the proxy assigns to a character outside [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. It is a stand-in for impossible, and it is what drives a token like '=-' deep into the blue.
Where the conditional strip becomes saturated red — the point past which nearly every token is base64-specific. The transition into it is gradual rather than sudden, which is the figure's claim.

By contrast, where the Arabic feature's conditional strip flips from solid blue to solid red in one step. The two strips are drawn the same way, so the difference in shape is the comparison the text is making.

The Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and this feature's activations, reported in the same section. The authors read the low value as a fault of the proxy, which also fires on hexadecimal strings that have a feature of their own.
The number of tokens listed in the inset's three label groups, left to right. The rightmost group is short because very few vocabulary entries reach the extreme of the tail.
